name: Diabetes Technology and Monitoring
blurb: Continuous glucose monitors, insulin pumps, automated insulin delivery and digital tools.
title: Diabetes Technology and Monitoring
answer: Continuous glucose monitors show glucose every few minutes and are now recommended well beyond type 1 diabetes, including for people on insulin or drugs that can cause low blood sugar. Automated insulin delivery systems link a sensor and a pump so insulin adjusts itself, and AI is beginning to predict glucose changes before they happen.

siblings.name: Kidney Protection and Diabetic Kidney Disease

explainer:
A continuous glucose monitor uses a small sensor under the skin to measure glucose in the fluid between cells and sends readings to a phone or reader. It shows trends and alerts for highs and lows, and the data produce time in range and variability reports that a single finger stick or A1C cannot.

Automated insulin delivery, sometimes called a hybrid closed loop or artificial pancreas, uses an algorithm to adjust insulin from a pump based on sensor readings, with the person still announcing meals. These systems have improved time in range and reduced hypoglycemia in type 1 diabetes and are expanding to type 2. Digital tools, apps and remote monitoring let clinicians review data between visits, and AI models are being developed to forecast glucose and personalise dosing.

developments.text: The ADA Standards of Care 2026 diabetes technology section recommends continuous glucose monitoring for people with diabetes on insulin and those on medicines that can cause hypoglycemia, and supports its use in other situations where it helps management.
